utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Brdjanin -- Could you call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. General Talic, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. General Talic, you may sit down. Appearance for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Susan Grogan, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Ms. Korner. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman along with Tanja Radosavljevic and Milan Trbojevic. And I'd just like to say that I'm becoming very worried about Mr. Cayley, and I hope he's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ackerman. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau, and I am with Fabien Masson. I represent General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Ms. Korner, yesterday just before we rose you made a statement with regard to the 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't have my list with me I'm afraid this morning, Your Honour, so I can't repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps you can come back --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After the break. What I wanted to know was the position with regard to Witness 7.118. You will recall that in our decision, we had directed the redaction of certain parts from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I handed that up to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And you've --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I've heard nothing back from anybody about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You handed the documents to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But I can only speak for myself. I have been through them. The only thing is that it suddenly dawned on me last night, sometime during the night, that I wasn't quite sure whether that was wasted time; in other words, whether this witness is going to be brought forward or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No, no. We accepted Your Honours' reactions as it were -- or the order that if we wished to put it in, we should redact. And so we did the redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But is he one of those witness that is you are not going to produce after all?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Because you said we could have him in under Rule 92 provided we redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And the other thing is in our judgement, there is a short reference to an objection raised by Brdjanin -- by Mr. Ackerman relative to a part of the statement where we didn't -- the part in which it is stated by the witness that Brdjanin was the president of the ARK -- of the ARK rather than president of the ARK Crisis Staff. And more or less we said that this is something that could be remedied either by a declaration forthcoming from the Prosecution that this is evidently a mistake or in some other manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, we said that in the -- in our response. But I'll certainly say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so. But in -- any way, I will check. But please do keep that in mind just before you actually produce this witness later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this witness will evidently come. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My position, Your Honour, is that it's not a mistake. It's evidence that this witness doesn't know what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Okay. But it is obviously wrong, you know, I mean, and that's something that -- rather than being redacted, it is something that can be corrected either through the witness himself or through the Prosecution in -- we even suggested that you could handle it yourself actually, but we can't expect the Defence -- anything from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rights of the Defence are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think if we come to an agreement rather than having to go back and take an additional one-line statement from a witness and the expense involved. But Your Honour, I think the only thing we're waiting for then is whether the Defence are happy with the redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. And perhaps if you could come back to Ms. Korner on the rest, both Madam Fauveau -- and Madam Fauveau in particular -- and yourself, Mr. Ackerman, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Monday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So having said that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just two matters, Your Honour. As a result of the complaint made yesterday that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because usually at the end of the day I lose count of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It was the complaint that the Registry appeared to be shielding AID by having lost all the relevant documentation. That's a joke, Your Honour. And I don't think Mr. Ackerman meant it to be -- or Madam Fauveau. We went back through our own files yesterday, and we have found the relevant documentation that related to that aspect of the Kvocka case. And this morning I have provided -- it's not formal disclosure, as I pointed out to both Defence counsel out of the goodness of our heart -- all the documentation that relates to that that we can find. I am -- that is not to say -- and I make that absolutely clear -- that I do object to the whole matter being dealt with, with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the second matter is this, Your Honour: Obviously we're all anxious to let this witness go today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do have some re-examination. I'm not altogether sure how much longer Mr. Ackerman is going to be, but I would ask perhaps that today we shorten the breaks so that it is possible we can get this witness away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I will take that into consideration. We'll see what the progress will be, because it also depends on how the witness reacts to the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And the third matter is that no doubt Mr. Ackerman, maybe others, will be delighted to hear they'll have Mr. Cayley next week and not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Having had a haircut presumably. Yes. Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Draganovic. Could we proceed with the solemn declaration straight away, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Judge, our apologies to you for starting -- for bringing you in the courtroom 15 minutes late, but we had some preliminary procedural matters to deal with, and we have concluded. Mr. Ackerman will be proceeding with his cross-examination. Whether you will have to return on Monday or not will very much depend on how you answer these questions; in other words, if you choose to give long answers, you'll probably end up spending the weekend here. So try to take my advice and answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were talking when we broke yesterday about your investigations upon your return to Sanski Most in the fall of 1995. In the course of those investigations, did you determine how many Serb civilians were killed when the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina captured Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't estimate that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you investigate that at all?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or rather -- in some cases, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to be shown Exhibit DB81 B, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect to this exhibit, I have already raised it with Mr. Ackerman. I'm not going to object to it being shown, but I do suggest that it has certain limitations. It appears to be pages from a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Similar to pages from books that Ms. Korner has presented, Your Honour. But I think when she hears the question I'm going to ask, she won't have any difficulty with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, her comment, remark, or objection -- call it whatever you wish -- goes on record, and then we'll see afterwards. Let's hear the question first.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will find if you get past the opening pages a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you -- before telling him what he will find -- tell him what this document is, please, Mr. Ackerman, without having -- without needing to put questions first. Tell him --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm showing -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where it originates from, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm showing you, sir, is a -- some pages from a book called "To forget is to murder the truth," published apparently in Novi Sad in the year 2000. The page I'm interested in having you look at is -- it's a list of people killed in Sanski Most, according to the book. There's a list of 23 people. The only question that I have of you -- I'm not going to go through each of those persons. My only question is: Do you recognise the names of any of those persons and did you conduct any investigation regarding the killing of any of those 23 persons?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about these names. Perhaps only one of the names means something to me; perhaps number 2. This is on the basis of the surname. But I'm not sure. Pero Grubor. I think that I carried out an investigation. I think so, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When the -- the army captured Sanski Most in 1995, what happened to the Serb population of Sanski Most, the civilians? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I arrived in Sanski Most, the civilians of Serbian nationality had mainly left the town. That was on the 10th of October. Most of them had left. That's the information I was given. And on the television in Germany, this is what I saw. And very few civilians of Serbian nationality remained in Sanski Most. I met those people -- I would meet those people in Sanski Most, but there were very few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to their homes? Their homes were looted then, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they were looted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you investigate the looting of any of the Serb homes?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember having done so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since -- since Dayton, have you made an effort to assist former Serb residents in getting their property restored to them and their return to Sanski Most? Have you helped out with that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, on numerous occasions, and I always do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you done anything as a judge to block the return of property to former Serb residents pursuant to the Dayton Accords, to keep it from happening?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just going to ask. I don't want to -- to what issue in the case these questions go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you'll bear with me. Trying to get through today, I could ask you to excuse the witness and tell me. But if you'll bear with me, it will be quite clear. I'm not off on some wild tangent, I assure you. And it's up to you. If you want the witness to leave and have me explain this to you, I can do it. If you trust me that I'm not on some irrelevant tangent, then I can go ahead. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead for the time being. And then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a pending question, sir: Have you done anything as a judge to block the return of property to former Serb residents pursuant to the Dayton Accords, to keep it from happening? You can probably just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that almost immediately after your return, you started looking for documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with regard to many of the documents that you have talked with us about here, you have told us over and over that the original is in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Part of the documents is in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct if I understood you to mean that there is somewhere housed in Sanski Most a collection of documents that were gathered upon your return to Sanski Most by you and others?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who controls that collection of documents? Who's in charge of it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents which were examined by an investigator from The Hague Tribunal -- so upon the instructions of the investigator, these documents are in the Tribunal. And the other documents which were examined in other institutes -- so not in my home, not in my house -- they're probably there. And I know what the purpose of these documents is. They're in the Tribunal. They are the documents in question, these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Somehow we got lost. You told me that there was a collection of documents in Sanski Most that were collected by you and others in 1995 after your return. My question was: Who controls that collection? Who is in charge of that collection of documents? Who has custody of it, that collection?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered that question. The documents that I handed over to investigators of The Hague Tribunal at the request of the investigator --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't asked you --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have these documents in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what happens, Judge. The question was not restricted to those documents which you showed or handed over to the Prosecutor or the investigators. The question related to all the documents that you collected after your return to Sanski Most. And the question is a very simple one: Who keeps these documents? Who is the custodian of these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my responsibility to keep these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you are the custodian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the simple answer. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your capacity as custodian of these documents, would you be willing to give an investigator employed by me, access to them, to look at them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So I will send someone to visit you whose name is Milos Peric and you will let him look at all the documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is Milos Peric?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An investigator that works for me.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to ask the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think this is at all suitable method of cross-examination, if -- the Judge is agreeing the details can be discussed later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, he's just seeking a reply from -- and he's had the reply. At one time he said, "Yes, at any time." And when he heard the name Milos Peric, he said he requires the consent of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what I mean. This is not suitable. There are matters that arise as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In my country, for example, there is no way you can seek access to criminal records, except unless you are the Defence counsel or the Prosecutor or the accused yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, there are matters they need to discuss with Mr. Ackerman about that. That's what I mean, there is not a suitable forum for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Ackerman will understand that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what Tribunal has to give him permission for us to look at documents that he has collected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But your question initially was in his capacity as judge, and a judge --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think I ever said in your capacity as judge, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Go back --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's been granted permission by -- the witness has said he can have an investigator to look at these documents. Arrangements will be made with Mr. Ackerman once the witness has finished. He's here as a witness now, not in his capacity as custodian of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with where we are. He said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. So go ahead. I think you should know where you are, Mr. Ackerman -- or you should know anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sometimes I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were searching for documents, you searched through municipality, you've told us, the headquarters of the SDS, police station, all of the government buildings and government offices there in Sanski Most I think you looked for documents in. You also looked for documents in some private homes, and one of those homes was that of Mr. Rasula, Nedeljko Rasula. How did you -- how did you get access to his house?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had access to Mr. Rasula's house. A soldier lived there, a soldier of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who had just moved in. I introduced myself. I said that I wanted to see whether there were any documents in there that would serve as evidence because I said that that was the house of the former president, and the man made it possible for me to enter the house. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how it was possible that a soldier of the Bosnian army was permitted to live in Mr. Rasula's house? Do you know how that happened?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the municipality would let people use such premises temporarily. He was there with his family, his wife.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the municipality basically took control of the property of Serbs who had left and then let members of the army and other people live in those houses; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the municipality temporarily took it over in order to put people up. It's not that they took anybody's property as their permanent possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you think perhaps the municipality was doing that to some extent in a way to protect that property and keep it from being destroyed until the owner was able to come back?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Who was with you when you went to search Rasula's house?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another gentleman was there. His name is Dino -- or rather Edin Aganovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a judge or a police officer or what? What was his official position?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had no position. He was attached to the municipality. He had to do with -- he had things to do with agriculture. He helped me detect mass graves. And I was coming back home from such a locality, and I just happened to stop by Mr. Rasula's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also searched other homes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very few. It's not that I searched private homes. Perhaps only two or three I was interested in, belonging to the people in positions of highest responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose home besides Rasula's did you search?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was in Radovan Stanic's apartment. He was a judge, president of the court, and he was an investigator of the Serb state security, and he was an investigator at Manjaca. I think I also searched the house of the head of the crime prevention service, not others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to Judge Stanic's house, how did you get access to his apartment?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The apartment was open, unlocked. Nobody was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with regard to the head of the crime prevention service, how did you get access to his house?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A family, a refugee family had been put up there. I introduced myself to them. I said that I came to look for documents -- or rather, I asked whether there were any, and they said there weren't any, and I think I didn't even enter the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the first day of your testimony, 23rd of April, page 4866, you were asked about companies in Sanski Most. And the question that I'm interested in and the answer I'm interested in was as follows: "By the time of the elections in 1990, how many of them, referring to companies in Sanski Most -- how many of them were privatised or semi-privatised?" Your answer: "By 1990, there was no privatisation. Those are all state-owned companies. Privatisation is only now going on after the war." Do you stand by that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this answer, is it restricted to Sanski Most or was that the case throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina that privatisation only started occurring after the war?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I want to say that privatisation started after the war, when the law on privatisation was passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm now going to ask you about an answer that you gave on the next day, Wednesday, 24 April, at page 4914. You were asked about the dismissals of Muslims from their employment in Sanski Most, and your answer is: "The dismissals of Muslims started early in April. I think after the 20th of April." And you then indicated that those dismissals were all completed by 15 May. That was a correct answer, wasn't it? That was the truth?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 15th of May, I was expelled from the court. Perhaps this went on for another few days. Bosniaks stayed behind in some of the companies -- we can say, say, until the 20th of May -- say the 25th of May at the latest, and then no one was left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were asked, sir, who ordered these dismissals, and your answer was you think it came from the Crisis Staff of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the Crisis Staff came into being, you said that it was Rasula and Vrkes who were ordering these dismissals; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff was established before the dismissals started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about the Crisis Staff of the SDS, is that a different Crisis Staff from the Crisis Staff that was headed by Rasula, or is that the same Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's one in the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. At page 4921, then, just a few moments later you were talking about the dismissal of judges.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At line -- well, your answer to a question had to do with the creation of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You said that you had gone and had a conversation with Rasula. And your words are the following: "I learnt from him that the question of the judiciary had not been resolved yet, and I also learnt that this matter was being resolved in Banja Luka. On that occasion, I also learnt that there was a Crisis Staff in Banja Luka which was dealing with these matters." That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this conversation take place between you and Rasula?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his office at the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And get as close as you can, sir, to the date for me, will you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Approximately how long before you were arrest? Because I think that -- that should be the starting point, point of reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This last conversation took place, I think, on the 8th of May. That would have been the last one. Around the 8th of May, around that date. I remember that they broke into my courthouse and they looked at everything, all the rooms, all the desks, my desk, the desk drawers. I think it was then. I made an offer to Mr. Rasula. I offered to leave that position if I was a hindrance and that he could appoint a different person to this position of the president of court. I offered that to him personally then, on that occasion. And I think that it was in respect of that that he said that to me that, this question had not been resolved yet. Was it then or was it mid-April maybe? Because when I got this letter, the threat, I was talking to him and I had the letter. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would put it closer to mid-April then, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps mid-April once, and the other time, as I said, round the 8th of May. That's at the office. But we did have some meetings together at the executive council of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you said "On that occasion I learned there was a Crisis Staff in Banja Luka which was dealing with these matters," I assume you learned that from your position, that you learned that from your conversation with Rasula. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you learn it from someone else other than Rasula on that date?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What Crisis Staff in Banja Luka was it that you understood was supposed to be dealing with these matters with the courts? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at document DB65 B, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Grogan reminds me helpfully that apparently this document has already been exhibited before as DB54. I don't know whether it wants to be exhibited a second time with a DB number. And I think it's also a Prosecution exhibit at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's back with a new number, Judge. Maybe we can do something about that at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, you have before you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have before you, Mr. Witness, the document DB65 B. And this is the Official Gazette of the Banja Luka municipality of 3 June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you turn just a very short distance, you'll come to a decision numbered 147, probably on about the third page. It's numbered 147. It's a decision on dismissal of a judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] On the second page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a decision of the War Presidency of the Banja Luka municipality dismissing Stojan Bogosavac as a judge; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Stojan Bogosavac is a Serb judge; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at -- there's a whole series, Judge, you'll notice of decisions here dismissing judges and appointing judges. And if you look at number 149, there's another dismissal of a Serb judge, Snjezana Petkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. These are judges of the municipality court for misdemeanours in Banja Luka. This has nothing to do with Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I totally agree with you. And this was 29th of May, 1992. If you look at number 150, the next decision, you see the dismissal of Gospava Joldzic, another Serb judge; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at number 156, you see the dismissal of Ljiljana Bosnjak, another Serb judge; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'd now like you to look at DB66 B. Some of the pages are not real clear, but I think the ones that I want to refer you to are. What you should have before you is the Official Gazette of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina of 30 June 1992. And I want to first refer you to decision number 218. And you'll find that on the right-hand side of -- I think it's - one, two, three - the fifth page.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a decision on the establishment of lower courts in the Autonomous Region of Krajina dated 16 June 1992, signed by Dr. Karadzic. And number 14 on the list is the establishment of the lower court in Sanski Most covering the territory of the municipality of Sanski Most. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. May I just briefly say something else? I consider this decision to be illegal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. I knew you would.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider this decision to be illegal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recognise the international law concept of self-determination, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at -- starting -- it's a little further into the gazette. It starts with number 232. You'll see a number of decisions electing judges to various courts. And the next decision I want to specifically refer you to is number 252. Let me know when you find 252.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In decision 252, Dr. Karadzic appoints a Bosniak, Smail Salihbegovic, Deputy Prosecutor in Bijeljina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 254, Dr. Karadzic elects Muhamed Gluhonjic, a Muslim, to the lower court in Bijeljina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 255, Dr. Karadzic elects Alida Madjarac, a Muslim to the lower court in Bijeljina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 256, Dr. Karadzic elects Alija Zvizdic, a Muslim to the lower court in Bijeljina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you now to take a look at DB82 -- DB82 B. I want to refer you to decision number 472 of this document. And this is a decision on the election of the president and the judges of the lower court of Sanski Most, dated 4 August 1992. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it elects Radovan Stanic as president of the lower court in Sanski Most. And then there's a list of other judges that are also elected to the lower court, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here; however, I haven't got anything on Radovan Stanic here on this copy. But I can say that this was an illegal election because according to law, judges were elected by the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that the declaration of independence by the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina after the Serb delegates had departed was also illegal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If you don't want to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Korner. I mean, I've already intervened myself. If you don't want to answer that question, you're free not to answer it. If you think you can answer it, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection is not based -- my objection is based on what relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. But I trust Mr. Ackerman so far. He hasn't been much at a tangent. So I think we'll stand a better chance of finishing today with the witness than if we go criss-crossing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise it becomes an argument on every question, Ms. Korner. There are many questions that one loses or doesn't see the context of. But it's the entirety of the cross-examination that one has to look at. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August of 1992, why didn't the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina appoint judges for Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. At that time I was in this camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you have seen Official Gazettes from the Municipality of Banja Luka, dealing with the dismissal and appointment of judges. You have seen Official Gazettes from the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dealing with the dismissal and appointment of judges. What you've never seen is any information in Official Gazettes or in orders from the Crisis Staff of ARK dealing with the appointment and dismissal of judges, have you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw the decision of the Crisis Staff and the appointment of Radovan Stanic as president of the court. I saw that decision. And it was read --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've misunderstood me. I was talking about not the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most. I was talking about the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You've never seen a decision from that Crisis Staff regarding the dismissal or appointment of judges, have you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it you learned that what Rasula told you about the Crisis Staff in Banja Luka dealing with the appointment and dismissal of judges -- when was it you learned that that was not true, that that was wrong?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never found out about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony on the 24th of April, page 4947, you testified about the 7th of May of 1992, when five policemen came to you and demanded that you turn over some foreign currency and some gold that was in the custody of the court. You recall that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that money and gold was in a -- contained in a safe, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the bank safe deposit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was in a safe deposit box at the bank, or was it a safe that you carried over to the bank and left there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was in a safe, in a metal box, that is. And then it was taken to the bank vault for guarding, for keeping it. The bank called Privredna Banka from Sarajevo, but I'm talking about the branch office in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, under the law, wasn't that money and that gold supposed to be kept in the SDK and not in some safe that you carried over to a bank? Wasn't that what the law required?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just, it's -- forgive my -- or our ignorance. What's the SDK?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's the public accounting service I think is what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that true? Isn't that what the law required?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony, you were referred to a couple of transcripts of radio broadcasts. You recall seeing those transcripts during your testimony here in court, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the transcripts here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what you told the Judges was that you knew those transcripts were accurate and that the tape of those conversations was accurate, because while you were in the jail in Sanski Most, you heard these broadcasts on the radio. That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now referring to page 4973, 25 April. "You heard those broadcasts when you were in a cell that was almost armoured. There was a small window which wasn't open which was covered with steel sheeting, so this sheet of tin fully covered the window. And on that sheet, that steel sheet, there were several holes made with nails. The door was metal, made of metal, so there was no air at all. The walls had turned dark from humidity. There was drops of water on the walls, and our bodies were wet with perspiration, and the walls had gone almost black. When I was put into that cell, they were yellowish in colour, and later on they turned almost black. Down the steel sheet that was on the window, the small window, there was also sheeting on the radiator and it was wet. There was water dripping from the body heat that was evaporating. For hours I would stand next to this sheet of steel, next to this little hole, so as to be able to breathe. Otherwise, there was no way we could manage. The same applied to the other people who were detained in the cell." Now, it was in that sealed, armoured, blackened cell that you claim you heard the radio; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And in any case, during the day, in the morning and in the evening, they would let us out to go out in front of the prison, to get food. And of course we would always listen to the radio. And the radio was probably based somewhere in the building of the command, and it was possible to heard music being played and these announcements. We could all hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was it you were taken out to get food? For how long a period of time? Was it -- were you out for like, an hour, hour and a half, what?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were never out for an hour. Usually it was five, ten, or 15 minutes. It depended on the people who were -- the guards. It depended on who the guards were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Usually it was about five minutes, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more than five minutes. Sometimes it was five minutes, and sometimes perhaps even twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 25 April, 2002, page 4988 and the successive -- the next page is where you testified about the burning of Mahala. Now, on page 4988, you said that you had heard the sounds in the night. And then, "On the 27th of May in the afternoon, they came, unlocked the door, forced us out of the cell, and let us out to watch Mahala burning, to watch Mahala on fire." And you say that was the afternoon of 27 May; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the very next page, you say this: "At 5.00 in the morning on the 27th of May, a policeman came who unlocked the door, and he was armed and he said that night they'd attack Mahala, and that's when I found out." Now, those things are different. In one case you found out in the afternoon, and in another case you found out at 5.00 in the morning. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the translation was, but I know what I said. After the shelling that night, at 5.00 in the morning Cetkovic, a police man came, called Dzo Banana, and he said angrily. He said that they had attacked Mahala, that the Green Berets were there and so on. So after he had stayed there for a while, the police and the army came later on and they let us out. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this policeman who spoke with you told you, as you just said, that there were still about 400 Green Berets left in Mahala who hadn't surrendered yet; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "There are others whom we haven't managed to control. There are a thousand dead, and there are about 400 Green Berets. And we are going to capture them and kill them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the testimony you gave at line 16 on the 25th of April, page 4989, was this, that he had said to you "There were 400 Green Berets left who hadn't surrendered yet." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then said just a couple of lines later: "I knew that there had been no resistance whatsoever in Mahala." Now, you weren't in Mahala that night -- that previous night, were you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in jail.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your house was in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it the case that you have a special reason to tell this Trial Chamber that there was no resistance in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no resistance in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you have a special reason to tell the Trial Chamber that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a very simple question, and it's just something that maybe you can help me understand. In your testimony about Manjaca -- and I'm now going to page 5090 on 26 April -- you were telling the Trial Chamber about that night when you contend that Omer Filipovic and Esad Bender were killed. That's what I want to direct your attention to. At line 18 on page 5090, you told the Judges: "Other people were called out too that night, including myself. However, I didn't go out, nor did some others go out." Was it the case that you could choose whether you wanted to go out whether you were called out or not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such moments -- well, I was so afraid, I wasn't even thinking. The doctor who was lying down next to me, he -- he held onto me and he said, "Don't go out. They'll kill you." And I don't know how I remained there. I didn't go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said others didn't go out either; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain individuals. One or two persons whom I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you heard people being beaten with -- these are your words -- wooden objects. You could tell that just by listening?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The blows were very heavy, very -- I heard strong blows. It's as if you were beating a carpet and you could hear each such blow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was could you tell by listening -- just by listening that they were being beaten with wooden objects?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you heard policemen running around with buckets of water and pouring it on people. That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you could tell they were policemen and you could tell they were buckets of water and you could tell they were pouring it on people just by listening?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I thought you told us at one point that the only place to get water was to go to a lake nearby and scoop it up out of the lake. Is it your contention that the policemen were running back and forth to this lake to get buckets of water?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I meant it. That's not the way I meant it. I didn't mean they were running all the way to the lake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You later heard from Dr. Derviskadic, who went out later that night and then came back and reported to you about things he had learned and seen, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a great deal about what you believe you know about Manjaca was based upon what you were told by other people, including Dr. Derviskadic.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he told you that three people were dead and one of those people was Senad -- is it Supuk?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that wasn't true, was it? Supuk was not dead.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained, Supuk remained alive. He fell into a garbage pit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At page 5115, 26 April, you were asked by the Prosecutor: "Do you know if anybody did get released as a direct result of any intervention by any high-ranking politician or military man or any sort of eminent figure?" Your answer was that you had heard that some individuals had been released, and then you went on to describe some of that. I'd like you to look, sir, at P330.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In part of the statement -- I don't know whether it's here -- but I said that I had seen Colonel Basara Branko. He came in his own -- he came and in his own car he took Nijaz Halilovic away from Sanski Most. I found this out -- I found out that he had taken him out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir. You're absolutely right. I didn't read the whole paragraph; because I only want to refer to -- when you said you heard that some individuals had been released. And now I want you to look at document P330, and I think you have it in front of you. And sir, this is a document dated 1 October 1992. It appears to be signed by Vojo Kupresanin. And it has a list of 13 people. And Kupresanin is requesting that those people be released by means of a pardon because it's been established that they did not participate in the insurrection against Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see this written document here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any of these people, any of these people listed in 1 through 13?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Biscevic Faik, under number 4. He didn't leave Manjaca right up until the 14th of November, as far as I know. He was then released with the help of the UNHCR and the International Red Cross. And I'm looking at the other names here. I don't know the other people. I can't remember. I know that Faik Biscevic is from Sanski Most. Perhaps it's an error. Perhaps it's his son. But I think that he was released in Banja Luka. But two of Biscevic Faik's sons were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those numbers that appear after the names, do you know what those signify?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you know, Mr. Kupresanin was not successful in getting these people released in October when he tried to do that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at now DB67 B. And this, sir, is another document that appears to be signed by Vojo Kupresanin. In this document, he's requesting that a person named Elvir Kesedzic be pardoned and released from Manjaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this, really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know this person Elvir Kesedzic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know Patriarch Pavle?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him. In fact, I know him from the media. I never met him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It appears from this document, does it not, that it was Patriarch Pavle who was trying to get Mr. Kesedzic released?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to move to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe this would be a good time to break. I'm going to a different subject, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have -- is it okay if we have -- we restrict the break to 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a break, resuming at 20 minutes from now, anyway. That will be 10.47 -- 48. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That's a record. 10.27 to 10.47, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Perfect. Absolutely perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. The witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Wait until -- okay. You can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to have Exhibits P630 and P776 together, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 776. You've seen them both, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's a question of having to find two bundles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look first at P776. And you were shown this the other day. And this is an order apparently from the Crisis Staff of the Sanski Most municipality -- Serbian municipality. It orders Judge Radovan Stanic of the lower court to carry out necessary preparations for the establishment of a wartime court in accordance with the state of war declared in the Autonomous Region of Krajina. You see that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at P630 now. On the same date, there appears to be a conclusion of the Crisis Staff as opposed to an order basically saying the same thing; they'll be in charge of preparing and setting up a war court in accordance with the state of war declared in the Autonomous Region of Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence that such a court, a war court, wartime court, was ever created in Sanski Most? Do you have any reason to believe that there actually was such a court created?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radovan Stanic as president of the court came to Manjaca. He interrogated inmates in jails as well as soon as they were detained. I don't know -- actually, I don't have any other evidence, because I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you did your searches for documents when you came back, you didn't find any court documents that would indicate that a court ever functioned in Sanski Most during that three years that was called a war court, did you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for Sanski Most that there was a military court there. There was no documents to that effect. But the military court was in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about a war time court, which these documents talk of a war court, that these documents talk about setting up. You never found any documents indicating that a war court actually operated in Sanski Most, did you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can put it that way, as far as the military court is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you learned this morning that on 16 June, Dr. Karadzic created a lower court system for Sanski Most, that order that you characterised as an illegal order; right? You saw that just this morning.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that no state of war was declared in the Autonomous Region of Krajina in April or May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look please at document -- and be provided with document P153. And we'll also need P371 at the same time. And keep those other documents that you have there in front of you. If you look at P153 --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. Excuse me. Just a minute. I've just remembered something in connection with the military court in Sanski Most. Some people from Sanski Most who were there and who were at Manjaca, that is, ended up at the military court in Batkovic -- or rather, when they went to Batkovic, there are even judgements from the military court. And they are civilians from Sanski Most. I've just remembered that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was a court operated under the authority of the -- of the army rather than a civilian court; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about a military court here. You asked me about a military court. You didn't ask me about a civilian court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I really didn't. I asked you about a war court. I mean, these documents say "war court." I don't even know what a war court is, but that's what they say. I didn't ask you about any military courts. I want you to look at P153. Do you have that? It's a decision from the Ministry of --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P153, a decision from the Ministry of National Defence in Sarajevo, dated 16 April, 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that document, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think he has the right document, Your Honour. Would you give him my copy of what I think P153 is. It apparently isn't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we all see what you think it is, by putting it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] A copy of the decision of the 15th April --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a 16th April decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. 16th April is when it's communicated. But it seems the decision was taken the day before, on the 15th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just don't know if we're looking at the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. This is why I'm asking you. My document Exhibit P153 has a translation numbered 01107402.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we must be talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's a decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But it starts at the decision on 15th April --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're right. It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The paragraph I want to draw your attention to is the second decision, which says: "A state of an imminent threat of war is hereby declared." And number two: "General public mobilisation of the TO in the entire territory of SRBiH is hereby ordered." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't say that. Is it this decision? It doesn't say that here. Perhaps it's a different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What -- judge, what number do you have at the top of that document? Is it 00574584?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's the same document. What you are being referred to is the second page, second paragraph, which starts [B/C/S spoken]. Is that correct, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, he's got it now, so I'm not sure. I can't say my own B/C/S version. It's the second decision, it starts with number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The third one, sorry. [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says, number 2: "A decision on other components."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. It's the next -- it's the next paragraph, number 1 and 2 that I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh. Oh, that's page 2. That's what it says in the explication. "In terms of proclaiming an immediate threat of war --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "An imminent threat of war and a general public mobilisation," correct? And this is signed by someone who is designated as the national defence minister, Bogdan Subotic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you look at the next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is which?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is P371. This document is a document dated 4 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document comes from the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, regional Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That is where general mobilisation is ordered, throughout the territory of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But nowhere in there does it say a state of war is declared, does it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document? I don't see it says that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a document I referred to when I was talking about translations the other day as a document that had not been completely and fully translated. And what is missing from the English translation is a translation of the -- of the stamp that you see at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And with your indulgence, I would ask the witness to simply tell us what that stamp says if he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ackerman. And Ms. Korner, I'll just draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm awfully sorry, I mean, I know this is all over the place. But resubmitting all these documents for retranslation is not going to work. They'll just go. The Translation Unit is up to its eyes in it. I will just have to hope that because it's been translated by witnesses, that will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Judge, can you enlighten us on that stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a stamp -- the old stamp of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It says that the staff of the Territorial Defence staff of Banja Luka. And also it has the coat of arms of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes. So this is not a stamp of the Autonomous Region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's actually a stamp of the Territorial Defence of the Municipality of Banja Luka, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's a Territorial Defence stamp. You told us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of Banja Luka, he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says: "Opstina Banja Luka" on it, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina, the regional Secretariat for National Defence, that's what it says in the letterhead. So this is not a document of the Municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the stamp, sir. I'm only asking you to tell what the stamp says, not what the document says. We know that.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that. "The staff of the Territorial Defence, Banja Luka."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Stamp number 1." But that's the old stamp. I emphasise that, the old stamp of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I was interesting in having you do was tell us what that stamp said. And you've done that, and I appreciate it. Now, when -- what Milorad Sajic is doing by signing this decision is simply carrying out the order contained in the document from the Ministry of National Defence in Sarajevo ordering general public mobilisation; isn't that true? This is not an independent decision but just a transmission of the decision from the Ministry of National Defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Which ministry -- in which ministry are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we started with document P153. I've gotten you confused and maybe everyone else in this room. We started with P153, which was an order of general public mobilisation of 16 April from the Ministry of National Defence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- to save time, if the point is that nowhere in these documents is there to say "we declare war," I'll take that. I'll accept that. Nowhere in these documents is there an actual declaration of war, notwithstanding reference to wartime staff and wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second point being that the 4 May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, did you take that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you still want to go ahead with the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's a second point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that is that the 4 May decision is simply an implementation of the 16th April decision, just implementing in the Autonomous Region what was ordered by the Ministry of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you need the witness to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. I don't think I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You can return all of those documents now, sir. And I'd like you to be shown P785. Sir, P785 is a document which you told us on 14 May at page 5551 of the transcript that it was signed by you as investigating judge; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's your signature that appears there; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what you see then on the next page is a list of 20 names. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you now to look at Exhibit DB79 -- DB79 B. And that seems to be the same list of names, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Except on 79 B there's a handwritten note up in the upper right-hand corner that I presume was written by you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And signed by you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document I want to refer you to is P --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just showing him and that's it -- what does the note say, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a pertinent question, even though it is translated in the English version not completely, because there is something illegible. Perhaps, Mr. Ackerman you could ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, it seems to me --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Microphone --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It seems to me that I have limited time here and that might be appropriate redirect but I don't think it's my job to ask Ms. Korner's questions for her unless the Court orders me to, and then I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Can I simply ask Your Honour where this version of this document comes from? I'd be grateful to be given that information, and I'll deal with it on redirect if Mr. Ackerman wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask questions, myself, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It comes from your office, Ms. Korner. You'll see the number down at the bottom 00511388 DOC/DSL. That's a Prosecutor's office designation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry. I'm not with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom of the English version of the document that has the translation of the handwritten, you will see 00511388 DOC/DSL. That is a Prosecutor's office designation. So the document comes from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on the B/C/S version, there is the same number, just beneath the illegible stamp and the witness's signature. So it presumably comes from you, disclosed number 68, I would assume -- or whichever, 66 or 68. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: P619 is where I want to go next, Your Honour. And the next document I'll want is P626 and then P164, just so the registrar can know where we're going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You should have before you P619, sir. And I want to refer you very quickly to paragraph 3, which reads: "Nedeljko Rasula and Nedjo Anicic are hereby [Realtime transcript read in error "authorised"] instructed to visit the leadership of the AR Autonomous Region of Krajina and explain in detail the situation in Sanski Most and try to obtain suggestions and guidelines for further action."

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The transcript says that they're authorised to visit the -- the document actually says they're instructed to visit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the transcript should reflect the language of the document is "instructed to visit."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two questions with regard to that, sir: You don't know, do you, whether or not that visit ever occurred?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was asked that question, and he replied to it before, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't recall that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other question, sir, is: If there was no Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on 21 April, 1992, then this instruction would not have instructed them to visit any members of the Crisis Staff, would it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at 626, please, will you. And this is a document from the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most dated 28 April 1992 which calls for the surrender of all illegally held weapons, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are conclusions of the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Serb Municipality of Sanski Most, held on the 28th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it orders -- requires the surrender of all illegally held weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
